title: Major Assignment #1
text:
Anyone who watches or follows League of Legends E-sports can agree on one thing: T1 is notorious for having a horrible domestic performance.
The team’s win rate is consistently negative, and it always looks like they won’t make it far through the finals bracket…but somehow they always do. In fact, they can’t seem to stop winning the whole competition. How is that?


Code
library(tidyverse)

T1 <- read_csv("T1_Team_Statistics.csv")

winrate <- T1 |>
  mutate(category = ifelse(grepl("LCK", tournament), "LCK", "Worlds")) |>
  group_by(year, category) |>
  summarise(win_rate = mean(result == "WIN") * 100)

winrateplot <- ggplot(winrate, aes(x = factor(year), y = win_rate, fill = category)) +
  geom_bar(stat = "identity", position = "dodge") +
  labs(
    title = "The dramatic difference between competitions",
    subtitle = "T1's win rate is significantly improved at Worlds compared to their LCK games.",
    caption = "Source: Games of Legends | Reagan Kahla",
    x = "Year",
    y = "Win Rate (%)",
    fill = "Competition"
  ) +
  scale_y_continuous(limits = c(0, 100)) +
  scale_fill_manual(
    values = c(
      "LCK" = "pink",
      "Worlds" = "purple"
    )
  ) +
  theme_minimal()

winrateplot









In 2024 you have almost a 25% increase in win rate, and almost a 20% increase in 2025. That’s far from an insignificant amount. Despite what a lot of people say, it isn’t luck (or magic) that gives them the sudden change in outcome. During Finals, T1 puts a heavier focus on game objectives, like dragons or towers, which when secured, boosts their chance for a win substantially.
But why do securing these objectives make such a difference? It all comes down to money, or gold. While not a guarantee, it’s pretty clear that the team with the gold advantage has a better shot at winning.


Code
library(tidyverse)
library(patchwork)

T1 <- read_csv("T1_Team_Statistics.csv")

bar1 <- ggplot() +
  geom_point(data=T1, aes(x = t1_towers, y = t1_gold * 1000)) +
  labs(
    x = "Towers Destroyed",
    y = ""
  ) +
  theme_minimal()

bar2 <- ggplot() +
  geom_point(data=T1, aes(x = t1_dragons, y = t1_gold * 1000)) +
  labs(
    x = "Dragons Killed",
    y = ""
  ) +
  theme_minimal()

bar1 + bar2 +
  plot_annotation(
    title = "The profit of claiming objectives",
    subtitle = "If T1 wants gold, it's pretty clear that securing these objectives is the play.",
    caption = "Source: Games of Legends | Reagan Kahla"
  )









Gold is an often overlooked factor in games, with the focus falling to kills or team-fights. While those are still important to the game’s outcome, a single team-fight won’t secure you the win.
It all comes down to T1 getting better items faster, which completely depends on securing those objectives, or gold, faster than their opponent.


Code
library(tidyverse)
library(ggbeeswarm)
library(ggrepel)

T1 <- read_csv("T1_Team_Statistics.csv")

set.seed(1234)

plot1 <- ggplot() + 
  geom_beeswarm(data=T1, aes(x = result, y = t1_gold*1000, color = result)) +
  scale_color_manual(values = c("WIN" = "pink", "LOSS" = "grey")) +
  labs(
    x = "T1 Games",
    y = "T1 Gold"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()

plot2 <- ggplot() +
  geom_beeswarm(data=T1, aes(x = opponent_code, y = opponent_gold*1000, color = result)) +
  scale_color_manual(values = c("WIN" = "purple", "LOSS" = "darkgrey")) +
  labs(
    x = "Opponent Games",
    y = "Opponent Gold"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()

plot1 / plot2 +
  plot_annotation(
    title = "More money, more wins",
    subtitle = "The bottom line is if teams want to win, getting the gold helps. A lot.",
    caption = "Source: Games of Legends | Reagan Kahla"
  )









So what does all of this tell us? T1 changes their play-style closer to the world’s season. During the domestic competition period, T1 places a focus on getting kills and picking advantageous team-fights.
As we saw in our first graph, this does get them some wins. But looking at this data we can assume that during the final’s season, T1 recognizes that the key to winning is focusing on objectives opposed to getting kills. While it may result in less flashy game play, it’s clear that it’s the best strategy for securing a win at Worlds finals.
